course: Daily Bread Sales: Bakery Production System

lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body:
Dough making and fermentation are the heart of your bakery. If you get this stage wrong, no amount of baking skill will save your bread. In Africa, where many bakers start small, understanding fermentation can mean the difference between a profitable business and daily losses. Fermentation is the process where yeast eats sugars in the flour and produces gas (carbon dioxide) that makes dough rise, plus alcohol and acids that build flavour. Without proper fermentation, your bread will be flat, dense, and taste like cardboard. With it, you get light, airy loaves that customers love.

Why does this matter for your daily bread sales? Because consistency sells. If your bread tastes different every day, customers will go elsewhere. Fermentation also affects shelf life. Well-fermented dough develops natural preservatives that keep bread fresh longer, reducing waste. In hot African climates, fermentation happens faster, so you must control time and temperature carefully. A dough that over-ferments becomes sour and sticky; under-fermented dough is tough and doesn't rise well in the oven.

You don't need fancy equipment. A clean bowl, a cloth, and your hands are enough. But you do need to understand the signs: when dough is ready, it feels soft, springs back slowly when poked, and smells slightly yeasty, not like alcohol. In this module, you'll learn exactly how to mix, knead, and ferment dough using local ingredients like wheat flour, water, salt, and yeast (or natural starters). We'll cover tools, step-by-step methods, common mistakes, safety, and a practical exercise. By the end, you'll be able to produce consistent, high-quality dough every single day, which means consistent sales and happy customers. Remember: good bread starts long before the oven.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body:
To make dough and ferment it properly, you need a few basic tools and quality ingredients. You don't need a commercial mixer to start. A large plastic or wooden bowl (at least 5 litres) works well. Wood is traditional and holds warmth, which helps fermentation in cooler mornings. You'll also need a clean cloth or plastic wrap to cover the dough, a wooden spoon or your hands for mixing, and a flat surface for kneadingâa clean table or a wooden board. A dough scraper (a simple plastic card or metal blade) helps handle sticky dough. For measuring, a simple kitchen scale is best, but if you don't have one, use consistent cups and spoons. A thermometer is useful to check water temperature; aim for lukewarm (about 30-35Â°C).

Ingredients: flour, water, salt, and yeast. In Africa, you can find strong bread flour (often imported or local brands like 'Snowflake' or 'Azam'). For yeast, you can use instant dry yeast (e.g., Saf-Instant) or fresh yeast. If you want natural fermentation, you can make a sourdough starter from flour and water, but that takes days. For daily sales, instant yeast is reliable and fast. Salt is important for flavour and controlling fermentationâuse fine table salt, not coarse. Water should be clean and drinkable. If your tap water is heavily chlorinated, let it sit overnight to dissipate chlorine, which can kill yeast.

Optional but helpful: a dough divider (to cut equal pieces), a proofing basket (or a bowl lined with a floured cloth), and a spray bottle for water. Keep everything clean and dry. In hot climates, fermentation can run away, so a cool spot (like a shaded corner) or even a refrigerator can slow it down. For a small bakery, invest in a digital scale and a thermometerâthey cost little and prevent costly mistakes. Remember, tools don't make bread; knowledge does. But the right tools make consistency easier.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body:
Follow these steps for a basic white bread dough that yields about 4 loaves (each 500g). You'll need: 1 kg strong bread flour, 600 ml lukewarm water (30-35Â°C), 20 g salt, and 10 g instant dry yeast (or 30 g fresh yeast). First, measure flour into your bowl. Add salt and yeast on opposite sides (salt can kill yeast if directly mixed). Make a well in the centre. Pour in most of the water. Mix with a wooden spoon or your hand until a shaggy mass forms. Add remaining water if neededâdough should be slightly sticky but not runny.

Second, knead. Turn dough onto a lightly floured surface. Knead for 8-10 minutes by hand: push with the heel of your hand, fold, turn, repeat. In hot climates, work quickly to avoid over-warming. Dough is ready when smooth, elastic, and springs back when poked. If using a mixer, knead on low for 5-7 minutes. Third, first fermentation (bulk rise). Place dough in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with a damp cloth or plastic wrap. Leave in a warm spot (25-30Â°C) for 1 to 1.5 hours, until doubled in size. In African heat, check after 45 minutes. To test, poke with a floured finger: if indentation stays, it's ready.

Fourth, punch down and shape. Gently deflate dough, divide into 4 equal pieces (use a scale). Shape each into a round or loaf. Place on a floured baking tray or in proofing baskets. Fifth, second fermentation (proofing). Cover and let rest 30-45 minutes, until slightly puffed. Don't over-proof; if it collapses when touched, it's too far. Meanwhile, preheat oven to 220Â°C. Sixth, bake. Score tops with a sharp knife, bake for 25-30 minutes until golden and hollow-sounding when tapped. Cool on a wire rack. This method works for daily sales: start early, keep notes on time and temperature, and adjust as you learn your local conditions.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body:
Even experienced bakers make mistakes. Here are the most common dough and fermentation problems in African bakeries, and how to fix them. Mistake 1: Dough doesn't rise. Causes: old yeast, water too hot (above 40Â°C kills yeast), or too cold (below 20Â°C slows it). Fix: Check yeast expiry, use thermometer, and find a warm spot (e.g., near a stove but not on it). If your kitchen is cold at night, use a warm water bath or an insulated box. Mistake 2: Dough is too sticky. Causes: too much water, not enough kneading, or flour with low protein. Fix: Add flour a spoonful at a time while kneading, but don't overdo it. Knead longer to develop gluten. Use strong bread flour, not cake flour.

Mistake 3: Dough over-ferments. Signs: sour smell, collapsed top, sticky and wet. In hot climates, this happens fast. Fix: Reduce fermentation time, use cooler water, or refrigerate dough after mixing (cold retardation). For daily sales, mix in the evening and let it rise slowly in a cool place, then bake in the morning. Mistake 4: Bread is dense and heavy. Causes: under-fermentation, under-kneading, or too much salt. Fix: Ensure dough doubles in size, knead until elastic, and measure salt accurately (2% of flour weight). Mistake 5: Bread tastes sour or yeasty. Causes: too much yeast or long fermentation. Fix: Reduce yeast to 1% of flour weight, and shorten bulk rise. If you want sourdough flavour, use a starter, not extra yeast.

Mistake 6: Dough dries out during fermentation. Fix: Always cover with a damp cloth or oiled plastic. In dry harmattan winds, place a bowl of water in the fermentation area. Mistake 7: Uneven loaves. Fix: Use a scale to divide dough equally, and shape tightly. Remember: fermentation is affected by altitude, humidity, and temperature. Keep a notebook. If a batch fails, note what you did. Adjust next time. Consistency comes from learning from mistakes, not avoiding them.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body:
Bakery work involves heat, sharp tools, and raw ingredients. Safety first: always wash your hands with soap before handling dough. Keep your work area clean. Raw flour can contain bacteria like E. coli, so don't eat raw dough. Clean spills immediately to avoid slips. When using ovens, use gloves and keep a fire extinguisher nearby. In many African bakeries, ovens are wood-fired or gas; ensure proper ventilation to avoid carbon monoxide. Never leave a hot oven unattended. For dough making, be careful with sharp knives when scoring bread. Keep children away from hot surfaces and electrical equipment.

Best practices for fermentation: maintain a consistent temperature. Yeast is a living organism; sudden temperature changes shock it. Use lukewarm water (30-35Â°C) always. If you use a refrigerator for cold retardation, allow dough to come to room temperature before shaping. Keep a fermentation log: record time, room temperature, water temperature, and how long dough took to double. This helps you predict and control. For daily sales, plan your schedule: mix dough at a set time, ferment, shape, proof, and bake so bread is ready when customers arrive. Don't rush fermentation with hot water; it ruins flavour and texture.

Hygiene: clean bowls, cloths, and surfaces after each use. Use food-grade containers. Store yeast in an airtight container in a cool, dry place; once opened, keep in the fridge. Salt should be dry. Water should be clean. If you have staff, train them on these practices. Also, consider food safety regulations in your country. For example, in Kenya, public health officers may inspect your bakery. Keep records of cleaning and ingredient sourcing. Finally, take care of yourself: baking is physical. Lift heavy flour bags with your legs, not your back. Take breaks. Stay hydrated in hot kitchens. Good safety habits protect your health, your customers, and your business reputation.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body:
Now it's time to practice. This exercise will help you master dough making and fermentation. You'll make a simple white bread dough, observe fermentation, and bake it. Gather your tools and ingredients: 500 g strong bread flour, 300 ml lukewarm water, 10 g salt, and 5 g instant dry yeast. You'll also need a bowl, cloth, scale, and baking tray. First, mix flour, salt, and yeast. Add water and mix to a shaggy dough. Knead for 10 minutes until smooth. Place in an oiled bowl, cover, and note the time. Let it rise in a warm spot. Every 20 minutes, check and record the size. In hot weather, it may double in 45 minutes; in cooler, up to 2 hours. Write down the time it takes.

Once doubled, punch down, shape into a round loaf, and place on a floured tray. Cover and proof for 30 minutes. Meanwhile, preheat your oven to 220Â°C. Score the top with a knife. Bake for 25-30 minutes until golden. Cool, then cut. Taste and evaluate: Is it light? Does it have a good crust? Note any problems. Then repeat the exercise, but change one variable: use cooler water (20Â°C) and see how fermentation time changes. Or reduce yeast to 2.5 g and observe. This teaches you how temperature and yeast amount affect fermentation.

For a real business scenario, scale up: use 2 kg flour, 1.2 L water, 40 g salt, 20 g yeast. Divide into 8 loaves. Time yourself from start to finish. Can you produce consistently? Keep a log for one week, baking daily. Adjust based on your climate. If you're in a coastal area with high humidity, you may need less water. If in a dry region, more. After a week, you'll know your own conditions. Share your results with a fellow baker or in a local business group. This practical experience is what turns knowledge into skill. Remember, every batch teaches you something. Don't fear mistakes; learn from them.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of fermentation in bread making?
options: B) To produce gas that makes dough rise
D) To add colour to bread
quiz.explanation: Fermentation produces carbon dioxide gas, which causes dough to rise.

quiz.q: Which ingredient can kill yeast if mixed directly?
quiz.explanation: Salt can dehydrate yeast and kill it if not mixed with flour first.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature for lukewarm water when activating yeast?
quiz.explanation: Yeast is most active at 30-35Â°C; higher temperatures can kill it.

quiz.q: How long should you knead dough by hand for a basic bread?
quiz.explanation: Kneading for 8-10 minutes develops gluten, making dough elastic.

quiz.q: What does it mean if dough springs back slowly when poked?
options: C) It is ready for shaping
quiz.explanation: Slow spring back indicates properly fermented dough ready for the next step.

quiz.q: In a hot African climate, how can you slow down fermentation?
options: D) Leave it in the sun
quiz.explanation: Cold temperatures slow yeast activity, preventing over-fermentation.

quiz.q: Which tool is most important for consistent dough division?
quiz.explanation: A scale ensures equal pieces, leading to even baking.

quiz.q: What is a sign of over-fermented dough?
options: A) It smells sour and collapses
B) It is stiff and dry
C) It has a smooth top
D) It doubles in size quickly
quiz.explanation: Over-fermentation produces a sour smell and weak structure that collapses.

quiz.q: Why should you cover dough during fermentation?
quiz.explanation: Covering prevents moisture loss, which can cause a dry crust.

quiz.q: What is the recommended salt amount for bread dough?
quiz.explanation: About 2% salt is standard for flavour and fermentation control.

quiz.q: Which type of flour is best for bread making?
quiz.explanation: Strong bread flour has high protein, essential for gluten development.

quiz.q: What should you do if your dough is too sticky?
quiz.explanation: Adding flour gradually reduces stickiness without drying out the dough.

quiz.q: How can you tell if bread is fully baked?
options: B) It sounds hollow when tapped
C) It is soft to touch
D) It is pale in colour
quiz.explanation: A hollow sound indicates the inside is cooked and airy.

quiz.q: What is cold retardation in bread making?
options: B) Slowing fermentation in a fridge
quiz.explanation: Cold retardation uses refrigeration to slow fermentation for better flavour.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep a fermentation log?
options: A) To track time and temperature for consistency
quiz.explanation: Logs help you replicate successful batches and adjust for conditions.

quiz.q: What should you do before scoring bread?
quiz.explanation: Preheating ensures the oven is hot enough for proper oven spring.

quiz.q: Which safety practice is essential when handling raw dough?
options: A) Eat a small piece to test
B) Wash hands before and after
C) Use bare hands on hot surfaces
quiz.explanation: Washing hands prevents contamination from raw flour and bacteria.

quiz.q: What is the second fermentation called?
quiz.explanation: The second rise after shaping is called proofing.

quiz.q: How long should you proof shaped dough typically?
quiz.explanation: Proofing usually takes 30-45 minutes until dough is slightly puffed.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of dense bread?
quiz.explanation: Under-fermentation means less gas, resulting in dense bread.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid chlorinated water for dough?
quiz.explanation: Chlorine can inhibit yeast activity; let water sit to dissipate.

quiz.q: What is the best way to store yeast?
options: B) In an airtight container in a cool, dry place
quiz.explanation: Cool, dry storage maintains yeast viability.

quiz.q: What should you do if dough over-proofs?
options: B) Punch it down and reshape
quiz.explanation: Punching down and reshaping can sometimes save over-proofed dough.

quiz.q: Which factor affects fermentation time in different regions?
quiz.explanation: Altitude, humidity, and temperature all influence yeast activity.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of scoring dough before baking?
options: B) To allow steam to escape
quiz.explanation: Scoring controls where the bread expands, preventing uneven bursting.

quiz.q: How can you test if yeast is active?
options: B) Dissolve in warm water with sugar
quiz.explanation: Active yeast will foam in warm sugar water within 10 minutes.

quiz.q: What is a safe practice when using a gas oven?
options: A) Light it with a match while gas is on
quiz.explanation: Ventilation prevents carbon monoxide buildup.

quiz.q: Why is it important to cool bread on a wire rack?
quiz.explanation: A wire rack allows air circulation, preventing condensation.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the practical exercise?
options: B) Mix flour, salt, and yeast
quiz.explanation: Mixing dry ingredients first ensures even distribution.

quiz.q: What should you record in a fermentation log?
options: A) Time, temperature, and dough size
B) Only the final bread taste
quiz.explanation: Recording time, temperature, and size helps predict fermentation.
